title: Practice Test 5: Claude Certified Architect - Foundations
description:
60 unique scenario-based questions using a different selection of 4 scenarios. All questions are distinct from Practice Exam 1, with no repeated content. Domain distribution follows official exam weightings across all 5 domains.

Each question tests practical judgment about real-world Claude deployments, including anti-pattern recognition. Explanations cover why the correct approach works and why each distractor fails, with links to official documentation.

Prerequisite: Review the official exam guide and complete Anthropic's free certification preparation courses (or have equivalent hands-on experience).

prompt.question:
SCENARIO: You are building a structured data extraction system using Claude. The system extracts information from unstructured documents, validates the output using JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) schemas, and maintains high accuracy. It must handle edge cases gracefully and integrate with downstream systems.

QUESTION: In the extraction pipeline, the "po_number" field fails schema validation on every attempt, even after three retries with the validation error attached. Investigation shows the value appears only in a separate purchase order document, never in the invoice being processed. What change resolves these failures?
answers: Have the model report a confidence score for the field and accept high-confidence values.
Raise the retry limit and attach more detailed validation errors to each retry prompt.
Include the related purchase order document in the extraction request alongside the invoice.
Add a prompt instruction stating the field is mandatory and must never be left empty.
feedbacks: A self-rated confidence score does not create the missing information. A model can also state high confidence in a value it made up. This option adds a filtering signal, but it does not fix the root cause: the value is not in the document that was provided.

Retry with error feedback works for format, structural and arithmetic mistakes. In those cases the model can correct itself from the document that is already in context. When the required value is not in the source at all, more retries or more detailed errors cannot produce it.

Retries cannot produce information that is not in the provided source. The value exists only in the purchase order document. The fix is to include that document in the context, so the model can extract the value from it.

If you push the model to always fill a field whose value is missing from the source, you encourage it to make up a value instead of being accurate. Anthropic's guidance says the opposite: give the model a way to say that information is missing instead of inventing values.
prompt.explanation:
The validation-retry loop is a powerful pattern, but it has a hard limit, and this question tests that limit. Retry with error feedback works when the model made a format, structural, or arithmetic mistake. In that case the correct information is in the provided document, and the specific validation error tells the model what to check again. One or two retries usually fix those cases.

The failure in this scenario is a different kind of problem. The value does not exist in the invoice. It is in a separate purchase order that was never supplied. When the required information is absent from the source, each retry spends tokens on a problem that cannot be solved, because the model has nothing to correct against. Retries fix how the model expressed what it read. They do not change what the model was given to read. The fix is a retrieval fix: supply the document that contains the value. A retry fix will not work.

The other approaches fail for related reasons. More retries and more detailed error messages improve a process that cannot deliver the answer. Telling the model that the field is mandatory does active harm. Anthropic's hallucination guidance recommends the opposite: it explicitly allows the model to say that information is unavailable, because forcing a value when the source does not have it leads to made-up values. Self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. At best it filters outputs, and it cannot recover evidence that was never provided.

See Reduce hallucinations for guidance on grounding extractions in provided documents and allowing uncertainty, and Structured outputs for what schema enforcement does and does not guarantee.

QUESTION: The extraction schema's "payment_method" field uses an enum listing "credit_card", "bank_transfer", and "check". Documents increasingly mention newer payment methods, and the model forces each one into the closest listed value. Downstream analytics depend on consistent categorical values. What schema change best handles these cases?
answers: Add an "other" enum value paired with a free-text detail field for unlisted payment methods.
Make the "payment_method" field nullable so the model can return null when no listed value fits.
Expand the enum with every payment method observed in production so far and redeploy the schema.
Replace the enum with a free-text string field so the model can record any payment method.
feedbacks: This option adds an "other" enum value with a free-text detail string next to it. The field stays categorical for downstream analytics, and the model gets an honest place to put methods that are not in the fixed list. New values are recorded explicitly instead of being silently forced into the wrong category. The detail field also tells you which categories to add formally later.

Nullable fields solve a different problem. They prevent made-up values when the information is not in the source. In this scenario the payment method is in the document, so returning null throws away real data instead of recording it.

Listing every value seen so far only fixes past cases. The next new method will be forced into the wrong category again. Without an "other" option, the schema stays closed and breaks easily when new categories appear.

A free-text field accepts any value, but it destroys the categorical consistency that the downstream analytics depend on. The same method would appear as many different strings. The goal is to allow new values inside a controlled vocabulary, not to allow any text.
prompt.explanation:
Schema designers use enums to keep a field categorical. Downstream systems can then group, filter and aggregate on a known set of values. The hidden cost is that a closed enum gives the model no honest answer when a document contains something that is not in the list. The schema requires a value from the enum, so the model picks the closest wrong label. This is worse than no answer, because validation cannot detect the error: the output fully conforms to the schema.

The standard fix is the open-enum pattern. Include an "other" value in the enum, and pair it with a free-text detail field that records what the document actually contained. The controlled vocabulary stays in place for analytics, and new values become explicit and easy to audit. Over time, the detail field shows which categories have become common enough to add as full enum values. The same idea is behind adding an "unclear" value for ambiguous cases: a schema should give the model truthful options instead of forcing it to choose a wrong label with confidence. Note that this is a design convention built from documented JSON Schema features (scalar enums and string fields). It is not a special API setting.

The other approaches each fail. Free text gives up the categorical guarantee that the analytics need. Listing every value observed so far still leaves the schema closed to the next new method. Nullability handles source data that is missing (where it does prevent made-up values). It does not handle data that is present but not in the list. Schema-conformant output guarantees structure, but never semantic correctness. So design the schema so that the truthful answer can always be expressed.

See Structured outputs for enum support and schema design guidance, and Define tools for required versus optional parameters in tool input schemas.

QUESTION: The pipeline currently prefills the assistant turn with an opening brace to get JSON from the model. Downstream parsing still breaks on missing required fields, wrong data types, and occasional trailing commentary. Which change most reliably produces schema-conformant extractions?
answers: Add a validation-retry loop that feeds parse errors back to the model until the JSON passes.
Rewrite the prompt to enumerate every required field and state that only syntactically valid JSON output is acceptable.
Define an extraction tool with the target "input_schema", set "strict" to true, and parse the "tool_use" input.
Add several few-shot examples of perfectly formatted JSON responses to the extraction prompt.
feedbacks: Retry with error feedback is a real and useful pattern. But it repairs failures after they happen instead of preventing them. It adds latency and cost for every malformed response. A strict tool schema prevents those structural failures before they happen.

Stronger prompt wording raises the chance of correct output in a free-text response, but it cannot guarantee it. The model can still add commentary, leave out fields, or produce invalid syntax, because nothing structurally limits plain text output.

When the extraction goes through a tool, markdown fences, extra text after the JSON, and free-text parsing failures go away, because the data arrives as the tool's input and not as free-form text. Turning on strict tool use (the strict flag set to true) adds grammar-constrained sampling. This guarantees that the tool input matches the schema, including required fields and types. Without strict mode, required fields and types can still be wrong.

Few-shot examples make the format more consistent, but only in a probabilistic way. They help reduce format differences between responses, but they give no guarantee. A text response can still differ from the pattern in the examples, so parsing failures are still possible under load.
prompt.explanation:
Structured output methods can be ranked by reliability. From least to most reliable: a plain instruction to return JSON, an assistant prefill that starts with a brace, a schema described in the prompt, and finally a tool definition with a JSON schema. The scenario already uses prefill and still fails. This is expected. Prefill controls the first characters of a free-text response, but it does not constrain anything after them. The model can still leave out required fields, use the wrong types, or add commentary at the end.

If you define the extraction as a tool whose input_schema is the target schema, the output arrives in a different way. The data comes back inside a tool_use block as the tool's input. It is not plain text that happens to contain JSON, so markdown fences and stray text can no longer appear in the output. On its own, though, a non-strict tool schema does not guarantee conformance. The model may still leave out required fields or use incompatible types. The documented guarantee comes from strict tool use. Setting strict: true on the tool definition applies grammar-constrained sampling, so tool_use.input is guaranteed to match the schema. Remember the limit of this guarantee: the conformance is structural, not semantic. A well-formed extraction can still contain wrong values. You still need downstream validation logic for business rules (for example, checking that totals add up).

The other approaches all depend on probabilities. A validation-retry loop is a valid addition for catching semantic errors. But if it is the main defense, you pay for repair rounds on failures that a strict schema-backed tool call would never produce. Stronger wording and few-shot examples raise compliance rates for text output, but they never guarantee compliance. See Strict tool use and Structured outputs for the documented guarantees and their limits.

QUESTION: The team's extraction prompt, used with an output schema that permits nullable fields, tells Claude to skip any field it is not confident about. On repeated runs over identical invoices, the same ambiguous fields are sometimes extracted and sometimes omitted. What change most improves consistency?
answers: Add a retry pass that re-extracts the document whenever an ambiguous field is missing from the output.
Strengthen the instruction so Claude skips a field unless it is absolutely certain about the extracted value.
Have Claude rate its confidence for each extracted field so downstream code can filter uncertain values.
Replace the confidence instruction with explicit rules defining when a field is extracted versus returned as null.
feedbacks: Retries help with format and structural errors. They do not help when the decision rule itself is not defined. If you run the same vague prompt again, the model makes the same inconsistent judgment about whether ambiguous fields qualify.

Making a subjective instruction stronger does not make it something the model can apply in a clear way. "Absolutely certain" can be interpreted differently on each run, just like "confident". The prompt still has no concrete criteria that the model can apply consistently.

Self-rated confidence scores are poorly calibrated. They do not stop the model from deciding inconsistently whether to extract a field. The variation would move into the scores instead of being fixed.

Vague terms like "confident" are interpreted differently on each run, and that is the inconsistency the team sees. Explicit, testable criteria give the model a decision rule it can apply. As a result, the same ambiguous field is much more likely to be handled the same way across runs.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests a core prompt engineering principle: explicit criteria work better than vague instructions. A word like confident does not tell the model what to do. The model must invent a threshold each time it runs, and nothing keeps that threshold the same across runs. That is why identical documents give different outputs. You can replace the vague wording with concrete, testable rules. For example: extract a total only when it appears next to a label such as "Total" or "Amount Due"; otherwise return null, which the schema already allows. This turns a subjective feeling into a decision rule that the model can apply with much less variation between runs. Prompting alone does not make an LLM deterministic, but clear criteria greatly reduce how often ambiguous cases change from one run to the next. Anthropic's guidance describes this as being clear, direct and specific: if a colleague with very little background could not act on the instruction without ambiguity, Claude probably cannot either.

The other approaches each miss the root cause. Stronger wording such as absolutely certain makes the instruction more intense but adds no criteria, so interpretation still varies. Self-rated confidence scores move the undefined judgment into a number. The model's stated confidence is not well calibrated, and the decision to extract or skip stays inconsistent. Retry loops are a valuable pattern for format and structural failures, where a concrete validation error lets the model correct itself. But they cannot fix a prompt that never defined the correct behavior. The retry only repeats the same ambiguous judgment with a new random result.

Prompts set policy, and the policy must be stated in terms that the model can check against the document it has. Combine explicit extraction criteria with a schema that allows null values for data that is truly absent. Then the model has an honest option and does not have to make up a value or silently leave the field out. See Claude prompting best practices and Increase output consistency.

QUESTION: Despite detailed normalization rules in the prompt, documents that state quantities informally ("about two handfuls", "roughly a dozen") yield inconsistent "quantity" values across similar phrases, even though every extraction passes schema validation. What change most improves consistency?
answers: Rewrite the normalization instructions with stronger emphasis, stating that measurements must always be normalized precisely.
Add a few targeted examples showing how informal measurements map to normalized values, with reasoning.
Tighten the schema for the quantity field with stricter type and pattern constraints to reject bad values.
Add a validation-retry loop that re-prompts Claude whenever an extracted quantity fails a format check.
feedbacks: Stronger wording adds emphasis but does not tell the model what to do. A phrase like "normalize precisely" can still be interpreted in many ways. The scenario already shows that detailed written instructions have not produced a consistent reading of informal measurements.

Few-shot examples are the most effective technique when detailed instructions alone give inconsistent output. Concrete examples that map informal phrases to normalized values show the judgment itself. The model then applies that pattern to new phrasings, instead of interpreting the written rules differently each time.

Schema constraints enforce structure, not meaning. The extractions already conform to the schema. The problem is that normalizations with different meanings are all structurally valid. So a stricter schema cannot tell a consistent interpretation from an inconsistent one.

Retry loops help when validation can detect the error, for example a malformed date or a field in the wrong place. In this scenario the inconsistent values pass validation. There is no error message to send back, so retries would almost never be triggered.
prompt.explanation:
This situation is the classic case for few-shot prompting. The output is structurally valid and the instructions are already detailed. Yet the model interprets ambiguous inputs differently from run to run. Written rules describe a judgment; examples demonstrate it. You can show a few informal phrases together with their normalized values (for instance, "about two handfuls" mapped to an approximate quantity with a precision marker). This gives the model a concrete decision pattern that it can apply to phrasings it has never seen. Anthropic's prompting guidance describes well-crafted examples as one of the most reliable ways to control output format and to improve accuracy and consistency. It also recommends making the examples varied enough to cover edge cases like these informal measurements.

The other options each work on a different layer of the system. Schema constraints and tool_use enforcement guarantee syntactic validity. But they cannot choose between two schema-valid interpretations of "roughly a dozen". Structure is enforced; meaning is not. A validation-retry loop is powerful when a checker can detect the error and send it back to the model. In this scenario every value passes validation, so there is never any feedback to send. And stronger instructions ("always normalize precisely") repeat the approach that is already failing: vague emphasis gives the model nothing concrete to apply.

Each mechanism has its own job. Schemas and strict tool use set the shape of output. Validation loops catch errors that can be detected. Few-shot examples carry the judgment that written rules cannot express. See Claude prompting best practices and Structured outputs for how these mechanisms work together.

QUESTION: On one run, two of the five source documents used to build one summary record fail to parse. Downstream consumers complain they cannot tell which parts of the summary are actually backed by sources. How should the synthesis output be structured?
answers: Annotate the output so well-supported findings are distinguished from topics the failed documents would have covered.
Have the model attach a single self-rated confidence score for the whole record so consumers can judge reliability.
Leave out the fields the failed documents would have populated and return the record with a success status.
Return a failure status for the whole batch and reprocess only after all five documents parse successfully.
feedbacks: Coverage annotations let the system continue with partial results and be open about the gaps. The completed work keeps its value. Consumers can see where gaps exist because sources were unavailable. Downstream systems can then make informed decisions about how much to trust each part of the record.

A single self-reported confidence number is an unreliable substitute for the real information. It also does not tell consumers which specific sections are affected. The pipeline already knows the actual coverage of each section for certain, from which documents parsed. So it should report that coverage directly instead of estimating it.

If the affected fields are silently left out and the run reports success, the failure is hidden from consumers. They cannot tell a value that is truly empty from one that is missing because a source was unavailable. Reporting errors as success is an anti-pattern that leads to bad downstream decisions.

Failing the entire run because two sources were unavailable throws away the value of the three documents that parsed correctly. Stopping a whole workflow because of a partial failure is a known anti-pattern. The more resilient approach is to continue with partial results and annotate the gaps.
prompt.explanation:
A synthesis step sometimes receives upstream inputs where some succeeded and some failed. The reliable pattern in that case is to continue with partial results and be open about the gaps. Produce the output from the sources that succeeded. Structure it with coverage annotations that mark which findings are well-supported and which topic areas have gaps because sources were unavailable. A gap is itself information. A downstream consumer acts very differently when it knows a field is empty because the source said nothing, compared with when it is empty because the source never arrived. So the output format must keep that difference and not hide it.

This is an application-level design pattern, not a built-in API setting. You represent the coverage status and source attribution as fields in your own JSON schema, or in downstream metadata that goes with the record. Anthropic's reliability guidance recommends letting Claude say clearly when it does not have enough information. It also recommends grounding claims in verifiable sources instead of filling gaps with text that only sounds plausible; see Reduce hallucinations. Anthropic's built-in Citations feature can also link individual claims to specific document passages, so you can audit them against the sources. But note the limit: Citations currently do not work together with structured outputs. A request that enables citations on documents and also sets a structured output format returns an error. So citation-based grounding must run in a flow without structured output, or in a separate step. Coverage annotations in a schema-constrained output must be your own schema fields.

The alternatives each break the pattern in a familiar way. Failing the whole batch because of two bad documents throws away completed work. It makes any single failure fatal, even though a partial-result strategy exists. Leaving out the affected fields with a success status is silent suppression. It makes an access failure look like an absence of data, which is the exact confusion the annotations are meant to prevent. A single self-rated confidence score replaces facts the pipeline already knows for certain (which documents parsed and which did not) with an unreliable, uncalibrated estimate.

QUESTION: A teammate observes that most Message Batches finish in under an hour and proposes moving the interactive document upload flow, where users wait on-screen for extraction results, to batches for the 50% discount. How should you respond?
answers: Move the upload path to batches but submit each upload as its own single-request batch to finish faster.
Move the upload path to batches with a synchronous fallback whenever a batch exceeds a few minutes.
Move the upload path to batches and poll batch status every few seconds to return results promptly.
Keep the interactive upload path on synchronous calls because batch completion times carry no guarantee.
feedbacks: Batch size does not create a latency guarantee. Even a single-request batch is processed asynchronously, with the same window of up to 24 hours. The API is designed for workloads that can tolerate latency, no matter how the requests are grouped.

With this design, every slow request costs both a batch submission and a synchronous call, which reduces the savings the change was meant to get. Users must also wait through the fallback window for every slow case, so the interactive experience gets worse instead of staying the same.

Polling only detects when a batch finishes. It does not make the batch finish sooner. Processing can take up to 24 hours with no latency guarantee, so frequent polling still leaves users waiting much longer than any on-screen flow can accept.

A typical completion time is not a latency guarantee. The Message Batches API has no SLA, and any individual batch may take up to 24 hours. That is unacceptable when a user is waiting for the result. So interactive workloads that block the user must stay on the synchronous API.
prompt.explanation:
The rule for choosing the Message Batches API is whether the workload can tolerate latency. This situation tests the difference between typical latency and guaranteed latency. The documentation does say that most batches finish in under an hour. But it also says that results become available only when all requests complete or after 24 hours, and there is no latency SLA. You cannot design a system around the typical case. If even a small fraction of interactive uploads take hours, those users face an unacceptable wait. So blocking workloads, where a person or a pipeline is waiting for the result, belong on the synchronous Messages API. The batch discount is for workloads such as bulk backfills, nightly runs and audits, which can accept the full processing window.

The incorrect approaches all try to add the guarantee back without changing the asynchronous design underneath. Polling the batch status more often only observes the delay; it does not reduce it. A batch can still take up to 24 hours, which is far beyond any interactive latency budget. A synchronous fallback pays twice for every slow request, and users still have to wait through the fallback timeout. This fails both the cost goal and the user experience goal. Making batches contain a single request changes nothing, because the no-SLA window applies to the batch whatever its size. The API is deliberately designed so that you submit work and collect the results later, which lets Anthropic schedule the work flexibly. That scheduling flexibility is what makes the 50% discount possible.

See Batch processing for the documented completion behavior and guidance on when batches are appropriate.

QUESTION: The pipeline returns schema-valid JSON for every document, but date fields arrive as "3/4/24", "March 4th", or ISO 8601 depending on the source, and amount fields sometimes include currency symbols. Downstream ingestion keeps rejecting records. What is the most effective fix?
answers: Add automatic retries that resubmit the document whenever downstream ingestion rejects a record.
Switch the extraction to a forced tool call so the output is guaranteed to conform to the schema.
Add explicit normalization rules to the prompt: dates in ISO 8601, amounts as a number plus a currency code.
Tighten the JSON schema with string pattern and length constraints that enforce standard value formats.
feedbacks: Retries that do not state the expected standard format only repeat the same underspecified task, so the model cannot know which representation to produce. Retry with feedback works for errors the model can correct. In this scenario the root cause is missing normalization guidance, not a one-time mistake.

The output already conforms to the schema. The problem is inconsistent meaning inside valid values. Forcing a tool call strengthens syntactic guarantees, but syntax is not what is failing. The mixed date and currency formats would remain.

The schema constrains structure and types, not the standard form of values. Concrete normalization rules in the prompt tell the model how to convert inconsistent source formatting into one standard representation. That is what downstream ingestion needs.

Fine-grained string constraints such as minLength and maxLength are not supported in Anthropic's structured output schemas. Unsupported features can cause request errors, and SDK helpers may remove them or move them into field descriptions instead of enforcing them. Even where a constraint could reject a particular written form, it cannot tell the model how to interpret an ambiguous date like 3/4/24, how to infer a missing year, or how to split a currency symbol into a numeric amount plus a currency code. Those conversion rules must be stated in the prompt.
prompt.explanation:
A JSON schema and format normalization rules solve two different problems, and a reliable extraction system needs both. The schema (whether supplied through tool_use or through output_config.format) constrains structure: fields exist, types match, and the JSON parses. There are documented exceptions, such as refusals, truncation when max_tokens is reached, and the fact that the casing of enum strings is not guaranteed. A schema says nothing about which of several syntactically valid representations a value should use. A string field accepts "3/4/24", "March 4th" and "2024-03-04" equally. So documents with inconsistent source formatting produce output that is schema-valid but inconsistent in meaning.

The documented fix is to state explicit normalization rules in the prompt together with the strict schema. For example: dates always in ISO 8601, with relative expressions converted to absolute dates; currency as a numeric amount paired with a currency code; percentages as decimal fractions; and so on. This follows Anthropic's broader prompting guidance: be specific about output format and constraints instead of relying on the model to guess a convention. See Claude prompting best practices.

The other approaches miss the real cause of the failure. Tightening the schema helps less than it seems. Anthropic's JSON Schema support is limited, and fine-grained string constraints such as minLength and maxLength are among the unsupported features. They can cause request errors, or SDK helpers can remove them and move them into field descriptions instead of enforcing them (as documented in Structured outputs). More importantly, even a constraint that rejects a particular written form cannot express the conversion logic the task needs. For example, it cannot say how to read an ambiguous date, how to infer a missing year or time zone, or how to separate a currency symbol into an amount and a code. That guidance about interpretation belongs in the prompt. Forcing a tool call strengthens a guarantee the system already has in practice, because the output is already schema-conformant. Retries that send the same request again repeat an underspecified task. Retry with feedback helps when the model made an error it can correct, not when the prompt never defined the standard form.

QUESTION: The pipeline returns null for "vendor_name" on 30% of invoices, although every document contains the name. Failures cluster on invoices that list the vendor in a footer table rather than a header. Which change most effectively fixes these empty extractions?
answers: Mark "vendor_name" as required and non-nullable in the schema so a value is always produced.
Add few-shot examples showing correct extraction from both header-based and footer-table layouts.
Add a stronger prompt instruction stating the vendor name is always present and must never be null.
Automatically resubmit the identical request whenever the extraction returns null for the field.
feedbacks: If you remove the null option, the model must supply a value even when it cannot find the real one. This encourages made-up vendor names. Schema design guidance recommends allowing null for this reason: it gives the model an honest alternative to inventing data.

The model fails to recognize the vendor name when it appears in an unfamiliar document structure. Few-shot examples that show correct extraction from each layout teach the model where to look. The model then applies that pattern to new invoices. This is the documented technique when extraction is inconsistent across different document formats.

Emphasis in the prompt does not teach the model where to find the name in an unfamiliar layout. The model is not deliberately choosing to return null. It cannot find the value. So stating that the value exists does not fix the recognition problem, and it risks made-up names.

Resubmitting the same prompt repeats the same failure, because the model still has no guidance about footer-table layouts. Retries help with format or structural errors when you send specific feedback with them. They do not help when the model consistently fails to recognize where a value is in the document.
prompt.explanation:
The failure pattern in this scenario tells you the cause. The data is in every document. Extraction succeeds on one layout and fails on another. So the model's weakness is recognizing the value across different document structures. It is not a formatting problem and not missing data. The documented fix is few-shot prompting with examples taken from each layout. Show an invoice with the vendor in the header and the correct extraction. Then show an invoice with the vendor in a footer table and the correct extraction. Anthropic describes examples as one of the most reliable ways to control output. It recommends that examples be relevant, diverse, and structured. Variety across layouts is what lets the model handle new invoices instead of only copying the samples. See Claude prompting best practices.

The incorrect options each misread the failure. Stronger prompt wording ("never return null") states the goal but does not teach the judgment. The model still cannot find the value, so the instruction either does nothing or pushes the model to make up a value. Making the field non-nullable applies the same pressure at the schema level. When a model cannot find a value but the schema requires one, it may invent one. This is why Structured Outputs guidance supports nullable fields as an honest option when the value cannot be found. Retries that send the same request again send the same prompt again, and the model fails to see the value in the same way. Retry loops are useful when they include specific validation feedback about format errors the model can correct. They do not help when the model consistently fails to recognize a layout.

Schemas and nullability control the shape of output, while examples and criteria control the judgment behind the values. When a field comes back null even though the data exists, the problem is judgment. So the fix belongs in the examples, not in the schema.

QUESTION: An invoice extraction fails semantic validation: the extracted line items sum to 145.00 while the "stated_total" field reads 150.00. The team wants Claude to self-correct on a retry. How should the follow-up request be constructed?
answers: Resend the identical extraction prompt up to three times and keep the first output that passes validation.
Include the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error about the mismatch.
Send back only the failed JSON output with an instruction to find and fix any mistakes it contains.
Add "double-check all totals before responding" to the original prompt and rerun the extraction from scratch.
feedbacks: Retries that send the same request again give the model no information about what went wrong, so each attempt is just another random try. Without the specific validation error, the model has no reason to check the totals that failed again.

This is the documented retry-with-feedback pattern. Claude needs the source document to check the actual values again. It needs the failed extraction to see what it produced. And it needs the concrete error so it knows what to correct. With this context, one or two retries fix most issues of this kind.

Without the original document, Claude cannot check which value is actually correct. It can only guess which number to change. To correct a mismatch with the source, Claude needs access to the source, plus the concrete error that identifies the inconsistency.

General emphasis is a vague instruction. It does not reliably change behavior, and it throws away the useful information the validator already produced. Sending back the concrete, specific error is much more effective than rewording the original prompt.
prompt.explanation:
The validation-retry loop is the standard pattern for extraction quality. Claude generates output, and your code validates it (with JSON Schema, Pydantic, or business rules). If validation fails, you send a follow-up request that contains three things: the original document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error (for example, "Field 'stated_total' = 150.00, but sum of line items = 145.00; re-check the values"). Each element has a role. The document lets Claude base its answer on the source again instead of guessing. The failed output shows what to revise. The concrete error points Claude to the exact inconsistency. Usually one or two retries fix these issues.

This case is a semantic error, not a syntax error. Structured Outputs normally limit responses to valid, schema-conformant JSON. There are documented exceptions, such as refusals or truncation at max_tokens. Strict tool use with strict: true gives a similar schema-validation guarantee for tool inputs. But even then, schema conformance cannot check that extracted values are consistent with each other or with the source. That is why you still need validation logic in code, together with error feedback to the model, even when you use strict schemas. The incorrect approaches all hold back information that Claude needs. Repeating the same prompt gives no information for correction. Returning only the broken JSON removes the source of truth that Claude needs to decide which number is right. And general emphasis like "double-check" is a vague instruction, and explicit, specific feedback works better than this kind of instruction.

Note that retries with feedback work for format, structural and arithmetic inconsistencies that the model can check again. They do not help when the required information is not in the source document. See Structured Outputs for what schema enforcement does and does not guarantee, and Reduce Hallucinations for iterative refinement, where Claude's output becomes the input to a correction prompt.

QUESTION: An extraction pipeline routes documents to auto-accept or human review based on the severity assigned to each validation finding. Arithmetic mismatches and harmless currency-formatting differences often receive the same severity label, so routing is unreliable. What change makes the classification dependable?
answers: Constrain the severity field to an enum of valid labels through a tool schema so only defined values appear.
Have the model report a confidence score with each severity label and route low-confidence findings to review.
Write explicit criteria for each severity level, with a concrete example finding for each level.
Resend each finding with the original document so the model can reconsider its severity assignment.
feedbacks: An enum constraint guarantees that the label is one of the allowed values. But it does not decide which value fits a given finding. The pipeline already produces valid labels. The problem is the judgment behind them, and schema enforcement cannot define that judgment.

Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and it does not define what each severity level means. The model can be confident and still wrong about a boundary that was never defined. So routing on confidence does not fix the misclassification.

Reliable classification needs clear definitions that the model can compare findings against. For each level, state what qualifies, and add a concrete example. For instance, an arithmetic mismatch is high severity and a formatting variation is low severity. This teaches the decision boundary, which the label names alone do not explain.

Retry with feedback works for format and structural errors, where the model can correct a concrete mistake. In this scenario the judgment itself has no definition. A second pass uses the same undefined idea of severity and can repeat the same misclassification.
prompt.explanation:
A severity label is only as reliable as the definition behind it. The model must decide whether an arithmetic mismatch and a currency-formatting difference belong at the same level, but nobody told it what the levels mean. So it invents the boundary, and an invented boundary changes from run to run. The fix is to turn the judgment into a rubric. For each severity level, state the explicit conditions that qualify. Pair each level with a concrete example finding that shows what belongs there and why. Anthropic's content moderation guide uses this same structure. It defines multiple risk levels. It pairs categories with definitions and with examples of what should and should not be flagged. And it links each level to a different action, such as blocking automatically or routing to human review. The same principle appears in Anthropic's evaluation guidance. It asks for specific and measurable criteria and notes that qualitative scales work only when they are applied consistently; see Define your success criteria and develop tests.

It helps to separate two failure modes that look similar from downstream: output with an invalid shape, and incorrect judgment. An enum-constrained schema fixes the first one. It guarantees that the severity field holds one of the allowed values. It constrains the shape of the answer, not its meaning. So a finding can have a fully valid label that is wrong. In this scenario the labels are already valid. They are only assigned inconsistently. That is a judgment problem, and only criteria and examples can fix it.

The remaining approaches also leave the boundary undefined. Self-rated confidence does not tell the model what high severity means. A model can be confident and wrong about a question it never received a rule for. Retrying with the original document works when the model made a format or structural error that it can correct. But a second pass with the same vague instruction draws on the same vague judgment and can repeat the same result. There is no error message that points to a rule to apply, because no rule exists yet.

QUESTION: The team defined an "extract_invoice" tool whose "input_schema" matches the target output format, but the pipeline parses the model's response text as JSON and fails whenever Claude adds explanatory prose before the data. What change makes parsing reliable?
answers: Add a post-processing step that strips leading prose with regular expressions before parsing.
Add a system prompt instruction forbidding any explanatory text before the JSON output.
Retry each failed request until the response text contains only the JSON object.
Parse the data from the "input" field of the "tool_use" content block in the response.
feedbacks: Regex stripping treats the symptom, not the cause. It also breaks easily when the free-form text contains braces or the JSON has unexpected formatting. The tool_use block already delivers the extraction as a parsed object, so there is no need to repair the text.

Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance. Free-form text before the JSON will still appear sometimes and break the parser. The documentation explicitly warns against relying on a specific text format when you use tools. The structured data comes in the tool_use block.

Retrying does not change the fact that text output may validly include conversational content. Failures will happen again, and cost rises with every repeated call. Retries are useful for correcting validation errors that you send back to the model. They are not a fix for reading the wrong part of the response.

When Claude calls an extraction tool, the structured data arrives in the input field of the tool_use content block, and it conforms to the tool's input_schema. If you read that field instead of the text content, you get the data no matter what conversational text the model writes.
prompt.explanation:
When an extraction is defined as a tool, Claude does not return the data as plain text that happens to contain JSON. Instead, the assistant response has stop_reason: "tool_use" and a tool_use content block containing id, name, and input. The input is an object that conforms to the tool's input_schema. The reliable pattern is to loop over the response's content blocks, check each block's type, and read the extraction from the input field of the tool_use block. This is why the tool-based approach is more reliable than asking for JSON in text. The structured data comes in a separate block that code can parse, apart from any natural language the model produces.

Anthropic's documentation explicitly says that responses with tools can include conversational text together with tool calls. It also says that application code should not depend on a particular text format. That is why stronger prompt wording or regex cleanup of the text can only reduce parse failures and never remove them: both approaches still treat free text as the place where the data is. Retrying has a valid role in extraction pipelines. But that role is to send concrete validation errors back to the model so it can correct format or structural mistakes. It is not a way to make the text output parseable.

If a team needs even stronger guarantees, setting strict: true on the tool definition uses grammar-constrained sampling, so tool_use.input strictly follows the schema. See Handle tool calls, Define tools, and Strict tool use.

QUESTION: Before each extraction run, the coordinating agent reads dozens of sample documents to identify layout variants. The raw document content fills its context, and accuracy in the later schema validation steps degrades. What change best addresses this?
answers: Switch to a model with a larger context window and keep reading all sample documents in the main agent.
Summarize the accumulated conversation whenever the context window approaches its limit during exploration.
Delegate the layout survey to a subagent whose verbose output stays isolated, returning only a summary.
Add a system prompt instruction telling the agent to disregard raw document text once each layout is noted.
feedbacks: A larger context window only delays the same loss of quality, and it costs more. Long contexts still have attention problems, such as the lost-in-the-middle effect. The large amount of document content still takes space away from the coordination and validation work.

Summarizing after the extra content has already entered the main context is a repair that loses information. It does not prevent the problem. Layout details and exact observations can be lost in the summary. If the long exploration is kept separate, so that it never enters the main context, the problem is fixed at its source.

Subagents run in their own context. The intermediate tool calls and raw document content stay inside the subagent, and only the final summary returns to the coordinating agent. This keeps the main context free for extraction and validation, which directly prevents the loss of accuracy.

A prompt instruction cannot remove tokens that are already in the context. The raw document content still uses space in the window and still competes for attention. Instructions change what the model is asked to do. They do not change what is in its context.
prompt.explanation:
An agent's context window is a shared, limited resource, and subagent delegation is the main design tool for protecting it. A subagent started through the Agent tool runs with its own separate context. All of its intermediate tool calls and the long content it reads stay inside that subagent. Only its final message returns to the parent. Anthropic explicitly lists codebase exploration, log processing, and similar long, self-contained investigation as the standard subagent use cases for this reason. In the extraction system described, surveying dozens of raw documents is self-contained work. The bulk of that content has no lasting value to the coordinator. What the coordinator needs is the short conclusion (a list of layout variants), and that is what a subagent returns.

The incorrect options all leave the long content in the main context and then try to deal with the results. Summarizing the conversation after the window fills loses information. Exact observations get reduced to vague statements. This is the classic problem with repeated (progressive) summarization. A larger context window raises the limit but does not change what happens. The same content builds up more slowly and at higher cost, and attention to the middle of long inputs is still weaker. A system prompt instruction to ignore the raw text does not change what is in the window. Every token the agent read is still there and still uses space.

Understand the design tradeoff. A non-fork subagent starts with a fresh context and does not inherit the parent's history. So the delegation prompt must explicitly include everything the subagent needs (file paths, the question to answer, the expected summary format). This small cost in building the prompt gives you strict isolation of the subagent's output. See Subagents in the Agent SDK and Claude Code subagents for the documented isolation and delegation behavior.

QUESTION: A team's single extraction pass over long multi-section contracts produces detailed output for some sections but shallow output for others, and captures a clause type in one section while missing it in an identical section elsewhere. Which TWO changes would most effectively restore consistent extraction? (Select TWO.)
answers: Split the extraction into focused per-section passes so each section receives full analytical depth.
Run a separate reconciliation pass that compares extracted clauses across sections to catch gaps and inconsistencies.
Rerun the full extraction pass three times and keep only values found in at least two runs.
Mark every schema field as "required" to force the model to extract each section with equal depth.
feedbacks: When one pass processes an entire long document, the model must analyze a large amount of content at once. Accuracy and recall drop as the working context grows. The result is deep extraction in some sections and shallow extraction in others. Splitting the work into focused per-section passes fixes that root cause directly, because each pass analyzes a limited amount of content with the same depth.

Per-section passes handle local extraction, but they cannot see relationships between sections. For example, they cannot see that an identical clause was captured in one place and missed in another. A separate cross-section pass applies the principle of keeping local analysis apart from a separate consistency stage. It gives the cross-section comparison its own focused context.

Majority voting over inconsistent runs does not fix the underlying judgment. Each run still processes the same oversized context and has the same shallow depth. Worse, requiring agreement removes real extractions that appear in only one run. This lowers recall instead of fixing consistency.

Required fields constrain the shape of the output, not how carefully the model analyzes each section. If fields are required when the source may not contain the information, the model is encouraged to make up values to satisfy the schema. This makes accuracy worse instead of improving depth.
prompt.explanation:
The failure pattern in this question is detailed extraction in some sections and shallow or contradictory extraction in others. This is the typical sign that accuracy and recall drop as the working context grows. This effect is sometimes called context rot. Claude's context window holds the document, the instructions, and everything else in the conversation. As that window fills, performance can drop even though the content still fits. This point is important: the context window is a capacity limit, but analysis quality is a separate, softer limit, and quality drops long before the capacity is used up. That is also why a larger context window would not help on its own. A bigger window lets you send more text, but quality still drops as the amount of content the model must handle grows.

So the effective fix is in how the work is divided. It applies the documented principle of choosing context carefully and splitting large analyses into focused stages. Focused per-section passes give every section the same limited amount of analysis work, so extraction depth stays consistent. A separate reconciliation pass then compares findings across sections. It catches the cross-section inconsistencies (an identical clause captured in one place but missed in another) that no local pass can see. This is the same way large multi-file work is handled in practice with Claude: local analysis in limited passes, and consistency across the whole document is checked in its own separate stage.

The other approaches fail for different reasons. Majority voting over repeated full-document runs combines runs that all have the same flaw. The agreement requirement also throws away valid findings that appear in only one run. Marking every schema field as required affects output structure, not analysis quality. Schema constraints guarantee that the JSON is well formed and has the complete shape. But when the model must fill a required field for a section that it analyzed shallowly, or that does not contain the data, it tends to make up a value. That is why fields should be optional or nullable when the source may not contain the information.

See Claude Code best practices on context management and splitting large analyses into focused passes, and Structured outputs for what schema enforcement does and does not guarantee.

QUESTION: The team exposed account operations through a single "manage_account" MCP tool that takes one free-text "instruction" parameter and interprets it server-side. Logs show frequent wrong operations: credits applied when the customer wanted an address change, and plan downgrades instead of cancellations. What redesign most directly fixes this?
answers: Have the agent retry with a reworded instruction whenever a result looks inconsistent with the request.
Add system prompt guidance requiring the agent to write more precise and detailed instruction text.
Expand the single tool's description with example instruction phrasings the backend parser handles correctly.
Split the tool into purpose-specific tools, each with its own input schema and defined output format.
feedbacks: Retrying through the same ambiguous free-text interface repeats the failure instead of removing it. For account operations like credits, a wrong action may already have run before the retry. Detecting the problem afterward is also unreliable, because the tool reports the operation it chose as a success.

Prompt instructions give only probabilistic compliance. Even perfectly precise text must still be interpreted again by the server-side parser. The interface itself is still undefined, so misinterpretation can happen again no matter how carefully the agent writes.

Better descriptions help the model choose between tools. But in this scenario there is only one tool, and the failure happens after the tool is chosen, when the server parses free text. Example phrasings make correct calls more likely, but the ambiguous natural-language contract stays in place.

The root cause is an unstructured interface. A free-text instruction has no contract that can be enforced, so the backend must guess the intent from text. Purpose-specific tools with typed input schemas make each operation explicit when the tool is called. The model's choice is then validated by structure instead of being interpreted on the server.
prompt.explanation:
A tool's input schema is its contract. When a tool accepts a single free-text parameter and the server decides what to do, the real interface is natural language. Neither the API nor the backend can validate natural language. The model may describe the customer's intent quite well, but the server's parser can still map that text to the wrong operation. That is the failure pattern in the logs. You can split the generic tool into purpose-specific tools (for example, separate tools for applying a credit, updating an address, and changing a plan). Then the decision about which operation to perform happens during tool selection, where Claude is strongest. Each operation's parameters are also expressed as a JSON Schema that the API validates before anything runs.

Claude chooses tools from their names, descriptions and schemas, and then produces a structured call. Your application runs that call. Structure that you build into the interface is enforced. Structure that you only describe in text is only a suggestion. That is why richer descriptions, stricter prompt wording and retry loops all fail in this scenario. Each of them still sends every operation through one undefined free-text parameter, so the ambiguity remains. Retries are especially risky for changes to accounts, because a wrong credit or downgrade may already have been applied.

Note the balance in Anthropic's guidance. It also warns against splitting into one tool for every tiny operation. It recommends grouping closely related actions behind a constrained parameter, such as an action enum. Either design is acceptable, because both replace free text with a defined, validated contract. The anti-pattern is the unconstrained natural-language interface. See Define tools and the Tool use overview.

QUESTION: To base policy answers on official documents, the team gave the agent a generic "fetch_url" tool for retrieving internal policy documents. Logs show the agent also fetching search results pages and third-party sites when answering return policy questions, producing inconsistent answers. Which change most reliably prevents this misuse?
answers: Replace "fetch_url" with a "get_policy_document" tool that accepts only validated policy document identifiers.
Expand the "fetch_url" description with boundary language stating it must only retrieve internal policy document URLs.
Add a denylist inside "fetch_url" that blocks requests to known search engines and third-party domains.
Strengthen the system prompt with a rule that "fetch_url" may only be called with policy repository URLs.
feedbacks: Replacing the generic tool with a constrained alternative removes the misused capability at the interface level. The agent can no longer fetch any URL it wants, because the tool accepts only validated policy identifiers. The unwanted behavior becomes structurally impossible, instead of only discouraged.

Stronger descriptions help when the agent must choose between tools that overlap. In this scenario, though, the tool itself can still fetch any URL. The description is guidance that the agent may still ignore, so misuse is still possible.

A denylist blocks only the misuse patterns that the team has already seen and listed. The open web has no limit, so off-task URLs that nobody expected will get through. Validating inputs against what is allowed is much more reliable than blocking what is known to be bad.

Prompt instructions are probabilistic. The agent may follow them most of the time but can still call the tool with other URLs in some conditions. When the capability itself is broader than needed, the reliable fix is to make the capability narrower, not to ask the agent to hold back.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the constrained alternative pattern. When an agent misuses a general-purpose tool, the most effective fix is to replace that tool with a narrower one whose interface accepts only the intended operation. A get_policy_document tool that takes a validated policy identifier cannot fetch a search results page, whatever the model tries. The invalid input is rejected before any fetch happens. This applies the principle of least privilege at the tool interface. A behavior problem becomes something that is structurally impossible.

It helps to rank these methods by how strongly they enforce a rule. Prompt rules and longer descriptions are probabilistic. They influence what the model is likely to do. They are the right fix when the problem is choosing between overlapping tools, but they cannot guarantee anything about how a single broad tool is used. Denylists are reactive. They contain only the failure modes that were already observed, and the number of possible off-task URLs has no limit. Input validation against an allowed set is deterministic. The capability does not exist outside its intended scope. Anthropic's own built-in fetching tool follows the same idea. It offers an allowed_domains restriction, because unrestricted URL fetching is a broad capability that should be narrowed when the use case allows it.

Well-designed constrained tools still follow the standard definition practices: a clear name, a detailed description, and an input_schema that makes invalid inputs impossible to express where possible. See Define tools and the domain-restriction options documented for the Web fetch tool.

QUESTION: You are designing how the "lookup_order" tool reports its outcomes so the agent can respond correctly when the order backend times out or when a search simply finds no matching orders. Which TWO behaviors are correct? (Select TWO.)

A generic status hides the context the agent needs to decide between retrying, escalating, or accepting a real empty result. Timeouts and zero matches need different responses. If you merge them into one status, you remove the information that recovery decisions depend on.

A query that runs correctly and finds nothing is a valid, useful outcome. It is not a failure. If you report it as a success with empty content, the agent can treat the absence of orders as a real finding and ask the customer for more details.

This is silent error suppression. The agent cannot tell a broken backend from a customer with no orders. Whenever the backend has an outage, the agent would confidently tell customers that their order does not exist. That is worse than reporting the failure.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the difference between an access failure and a valid empty result. In an access failure, the tool could not do its job (for example, a backend timeout). In a valid empty result, the tool did its job and the real answer is "nothing matched". At first, the two outcomes look alike, because in both cases there is no data. But they need opposite responses from the agent. A timeout needs a retry or an escalation. An empty match list is a real finding that the agent should act on, for example by asking the customer to confirm the order number.

The tool result contract states explicitly how to signal this difference. A failed execution should be reported with the error flag set, is_error: true, together with a descriptive message, so Claude can reason about how to recover. The Agent SDK documentation specifically recommends catching network failures and non-200 responses in custom tool handlers and returning them as error results. A raw exception should not be the only signal. On the other side, the Messages API documents an empty tool result (a result with no content and no error flag) as a valid success. So empty content alone must never be read as a failure.

The two incorrect behaviors are documented anti-patterns. Marking a timeout as a successful empty result is silent suppression. During every backend incident, the agent, and in the end the customer, receives a confident but false "no orders found" answer. Merging both outcomes into a generic status removes the context that recovery logic depends on. The agent can no longer decide whether to retry, escalate or accept the result, because the signal that tells those cases apart was removed at the source.

Sometimes an agent escalates in the middle of a process to a human who cannot see the conversation. In that case the escalation payload is the only way the state of the case reaches the human. The reliable place to enforce this is the input schema of the escalate_to_human tool. If those fields are required, every escalation call must supply them, and the application can validate the payload before it creates the ticket. This is the same difference between deterministic and probabilistic methods that appears throughout agent architecture. A schema (optionally combined with strict tool use, which forces tool inputs to match the declared JSON Schema) enforces structure in the protocol itself. A system prompt instruction to "write detailed notes" only makes compliance more likely.

Passing along raw tool outputs gives the human evidence without analysis, so the human must rebuild the reasoning the agent already did. Keep "tool_choice" as "auto" and add a system prompt rule that "get_customer" always runs first.

feedbacks: Forced tool selection, with a type of "tool" and an explicit tool name, requires Claude to call that specific tool on that turn. This is the only tool_choice mode that guarantees a particular named tool runs. So it is the right mechanism to make sure get_customer is called, instead of a text answer or a different tool.

Strict tool use makes the tool's inputs match its JSON schema. It does not require Claude to call the tool at all. Controlling which tool is called is the job of tool_choice, not of the strict flag on a tool definition.

With "auto", Claude decides whether to call any tool at all. Prompt instructions are probabilistic, not enforced. The model may still answer in text or call a different tool, so this approach cannot guarantee the required first step.

The "any" setting guarantees that some tool is called, but Claude still chooses which one. The agent could meet this requirement by calling lookup_order or process_refund instead. So it does not guarantee that get_customer is the tool that is called.
prompt.explanation:
The tool_choice parameter is the API-level control over whether and how Claude uses tools on a given turn. Its modes give stronger and stronger guarantees. With auto (the default when tools are provided), Claude decides freely: it may call a tool or answer in plain text. With any, Claude must call some tool, but the model still chooses which of the available tools to call. Only forced selection, written as {"type": "tool", "name": "get_customer"}, requires a specific named tool to be called. That is what a required first step like identity verification needs.

The key idea is the difference between probabilistic guidance and deterministic enforcement. A system prompt rule under auto only makes the behavior more likely. When skipping a step can lead to a refund going to the wrong person, that is not enough. The any setting looks like an attractive middle option, because it does guarantee structured output. But in this scenario it guarantees the wrong thing: a tool call, not the tool call. And strict: true on a tool definition solves a completely separate problem. It makes the tool's inputs schema-valid once the tool is chosen. It has no effect on whether the tool is chosen at all.

Note some limits when you use forced tool use. When tool_choice is any or tool, the API prefills the assistant message to force the call. So the model will not write any natural-language explanation before the tool_use block. If you want conversational text plus a strong preference for one tool, the documented pattern is auto with an explicit prompt instruction. Parallel tool use is on by default. So forcing a named tool guarantees that this tool runs, but not that it is the only call on the turn. Setting disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside tool_choice limits this to exactly one call. Finally, not all configurations support forced modes. Certain models and manual extended thinking reject any and tool, while auto still works. QUESTION: The agent outputs a confidence score with each automated resolution, and overall accuracy measures 96%. Leadership wants to stop human review of high-confidence cases. Which TWO practices should be in place before making this change? (Select TWO.)
answers: Break accuracy down by request type and extracted field instead of trusting the aggregate figure.
Have the agent re-rate its own confidence after drafting each resolution and route on that rating.
Audit a stratified random sample of high-confidence resolutions regularly to detect new error patterns.
Raise the confidence threshold for automation and accept the aggregate accuracy as sufficient evidence.
feedbacks: An overall 96% can hide serious weakness in a specific segment, such as billing disputes or a particular field, where errors are concentrated. Checking accuracy for each segment confirms that performance is stable everywhere before human review is reduced.

Self-reported confidence is an unreliable substitute for measured accuracy, because the model is often confident and wrong on the hard cases. A second self-rating pass does not give the independent measurement that you get from sampling against ground truth.

Even high-confidence outputs can contain errors that the confidence score does not predict. This is especially true for new failure modes that appear after deployment. Stratified random sampling within the high-confidence segment is the mechanism that catches these rare but important errors before they build up without anyone noticing.

A higher threshold reduces how many cases are automated. But it does not check that the confidence scores are calibrated, or that accuracy holds across segments. The overall figure can still hide poor performance on specific request types, so this gives no real validation.
prompt.explanation:
Before you remove human oversight from any segment of an automated workflow, the core question is whether the metric that justifies the change actually measures what matters. An overall accuracy number is a weighted average. Suppose billing disputes are 10% of traffic and the agent fails on 40% of them. The system can still report 96% overall while it consistently mishandles a whole category. That is why accuracy must be checked by segment (request type, field, document type) before review is reduced for any of them.

The second safeguard is stratified random sampling of the high-confidence cases themselves. Confidence scores are an output of your application. The platform does not calibrate or guarantee them. They tend to fail on the cases where the model is wrong but sure of itself. The only way to detect new error patterns is to keep auditing a random part of the "trusted" outputs against ground truth. These are failure modes that did not exist in the original validation set, and no threshold tuning could predict them. Anthropic's evaluation guidance reflects the same idea. Success criteria should have multiple dimensions, and eval sets should match the real task distribution, including edge cases, instead of reducing quality to one number (Develop test cases).

The incorrect approaches have a shared flaw: they add mechanisms without adding measurement. Raising the confidence threshold only makes the automated set smaller, while it still trusts an overall figure that nobody validated. Having the model re-rate its own confidence replaces independent verification with a measure that is known to be unreliable. Production classification guidance instead combines confidence-based routing with continuous monitoring and regular evaluation, using metrics like precision and recall. This way automation decisions stay based on measured performance for each segment (Content moderation guide).

The documented format for a parallel batch is one tool result per tool call, all sent together in the single next message. This correctly completes the parallel calls: the application runs both and returns both results together. It also keeps the model making batched calls in future turns.

Parallel delegation means that multiple tool call blocks appear in one assistant turn. The documentation explicitly says that returning results in separate messages, one per subagent, is the wrong format for parallel tool use. It breaks the exchange into sequential turns. It also teaches the model not to batch independent calls together.

When Claude decides that two pieces of work are independent, it can produce several tool call blocks in one response, with stop_reason set to tool_use. Your orchestration code then decides how to run that batch. Independent, read-only investigations, like a billing lookup and a return check, are safe to run at the same time. Operations that depend on order, or that have side effects, may still need to run one after another. The model proposes the batch and the harness schedules it.

The protocol has a matching rule for the results. Every tool call in the batch must receive exactly one tool result block. All of those results must come back together in the single next message, before any text content. If one subagent fails or is skipped, you still return a matching result with is_error set to true. It also teaches the model, through the conversation history, that calls happen one at a time, and this reduces batching in future turns.

feedbacks: A clearer message may reduce the wasted retries. But it still presents a successful query as a failure. The agent would probably apologize or escalate over a condition that is not an error at all, instead of telling the customer that no orders exist.

This asks the prompt to make up for a misleading tool interface, and compliance with such instructions is probabilistic. The root cause is that the tool labels a valid empty result as an error. That should be fixed at the interface level.

A customer with no orders is a valid query result, not a failure. Returning success with an empty list tells the agent that the lookup worked and that there is nothing to find. The agent can then tell the customer directly, instead of retrying or escalating.

prompt.explanation:

The agent never learned the answer, so it makes sense to decide whether to retry. A query that completes and finds nothing is a successful operation, and its answer is empty. The current tool mixes up the two, because it sets isError: true for a no-match result. This gives the agent false information. The agent believes the lookup never succeeded, so it retries and finally escalates a case it could have resolved by telling the customer there are no orders on record.

Error signals exist to guide recovery decisions. The MCP specification tells servers to report tool execution failures that the model can act on inside tool results with isError: true, so that the model can correct itself. That mechanism works only if the flag is used only for real failures. Returning a successful result with an empty list gives the agent an accurate picture of the situation. First-contact resolution depends on that.

Keeping the error flag while writing a clearer message still presents a normal result as a failure, which pushes the agent toward an apology or an escalation. A system prompt rule asks probabilistic instruction-following to hide a misleading interface, when the fix belongs in the tool contract itself. Broadening search parameters treats an accurate empty answer as bad input. It invites the agent to loosen the matching and possibly return the wrong customer's orders.

The receiving human cannot see the transcript. So a payload validated against a schema is the reliable way to make sure that nothing essential is left out without anyone noticing.

The model's self-rated confidence is an unreliable measure of summary quality, and it cannot guarantee that required fields are present. Holding back handoffs with low scores also risks blocking escalations that really need a human. That is the opposite of what the escalation path is for.

Anthropic's documentation says that JSON schema definitions may be cached for up to 24 hours. Values that belong to a specific case go in the generated output, which is processed with zero data retention.

A handoff to a human who cannot see the conversation transcript must be a complete, structured document on its own. Two separate concerns control its design: completeness and data safety. Completeness is best handled with structured outputs. You supply a JSON schema that marks customer ID, root cause, refund amount and recommended action as required fields. The model's output is then forced into that shape, so a handoff without a refund amount cannot reach the queue unnoticed. Without this, you can only hope the model follows the prompt that asked for those fields, which is probabilistic. With it, you have a validated contract that downstream routing code and human agents can depend on.

Data safety is the less obvious concern. Prompts and responses for structured outputs are processed with zero data retention. But Anthropic's documentation warns that the JSON schema itself may be cached for up to 24 hours. That is why sensitive values, such as customer identifiers and dollar amounts, must appear only in message content and generated output. They must never be built into schema property names, enum values, const values, or regex patterns. The schema describes the shape of a handoff. The output contains the facts of the specific case.

The other approaches fail for predictable reasons. Sending the full transcript and raw tool results replaces a selected summary with large amounts of unneeded data. Context-window guidance notes that recall drops as volume grows. A human who is triaging a queue needs the state of the case, not a replay of the investigation. Anthropic recommends detailed descriptions that cover what the tool does, its parameters, its outputs and its caveats. It notes that one-sentence descriptions leave the model guessing. If you document the inputs, the return values, and constraints such as approval requirements, the model gets the information it needs to route refunds and disputes correctly.

Descriptions are the main mechanism Claude uses to choose among tools, and wrong tool selection is usually caused by ambiguous descriptions. If you add explicit language that tells the tools apart by when to use each one, you fix the overlap that causes the wrong routing.

It recommends making descriptions more precise, so that they tell tools apart by when to use each one, not only by what each one does. Set the definition's "tools" field to only "get_customer" and "lookup_order", omitting "process_refund".
Omit the "tools" field and state in the subagent's system prompt that it must never issue refunds.
