feedbacks: The description affects when Claude delegates a task to this subagent. It does not limit which tools the subagent can call once it is running. A subagent described as investigative could still call process_refund if the tool is still in its tool set.

The tools field is an allowlist. When it is present, the subagent receives only the listed tools, so process_refund does not exist in its session. This is a structural guarantee, not an instruction that the model might ignore.

If you omit the tools field, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents, including process_refund. A system prompt instruction gives only probabilistic compliance, so the forbidden tool could still be called.
No such inheritance mechanism exists. When the tools field is omitted, a subagent inherits the full set of tools available to subagents, no matter what the coordinator has recently called.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent type is configured through an AgentDefinition. Its required fields are description and prompt, and it has an optional tools field that works as an allowlist. The three fields do different jobs, and the exam expects you to keep them apart. The description tells Claude when to delegate to this subagent. The prompt controls how it behaves once it is running. And tools decides what it can actually do. Only the last one is enforced structurally.

If you list only get_customer and lookup_order in tools, process_refund is never given to the subagent at all. It cannot be called, because it is not in the session. This follows the principle of least privilege, the same reasoning behind the documented read-only tool sets like Read, Grep, and Glob for analysis agents. By contrast, if you omit tools, the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. Then a prompt instruction that forbids refunds would be the only barrier, and prompt instructions are probabilistic. Changing the description affects only routing decisions, not tool access at runtime. And there is no mechanism that makes a subagent inherit only the tools its parent recently used.

Register the experimental log-parsing server with user scope so it is stored in "~/.claude.json" and stays private.

If the team server is in each engineer's user-level file, every person must configure it by hand, and the setup is not in version control. Configurations then become different over time, and new teammates get nothing when they clone. Project scope with a committed .mcp.json exists to avoid this setup work for each developer.

This file is meant to be checked into version control, so every contributor who clones or pulls the project connects to the same servers with no manual setup. User scope writes the entry to ~/.claude.json in the home directory. There it is private to one account but available in all of that person's projects. This design is deliberate. Team tools should be stored with the code, so the whole team works with identical integrations. Personal experiments should stay out of the shared configuration until they are ready to be shared.

Provide the entire module in one large prompt so the agent can plan all tests in a single pass.

feedbacks: Dynamic adaptive decomposition is the documented pattern for open-ended investigation where the full scope is not known at the start. The agent maps the structure first. Then it sets priorities based on what it finds. It also adapts when it discovers something, such as an external dependency, that needs a new subtask, such as adding a mock.

A larger input does not solve the real problem: the needed work only becomes clear through exploration. A single large pass also spreads the model's attention across the whole module. It also cannot adapt to discoveries, such as undocumented dependencies that need mocks.

Prompt chaining fits predictable tasks that split clearly into fixed subtasks known in advance, such as a standard review that checks several aspects. In this scenario, the subtasks cannot be predicted before exploration. A predefined pipeline would miss work that the agent only discovers along the way.

Confidence self-ratings are an unreliable measure. They also address output quality, not how the task is broken down. The main challenge in this scenario is that the subtasks themselves are unknown until the agent explores. Retrying low-confidence steps does nothing to solve that.
prompt.explanation:
Anthropic's agent-design guidance makes a clear distinction between workflows and more dynamic approaches. In a workflow, LLM calls follow predefined code paths. In a dynamic approach, the model directs its own process. Prompt chaining is on the workflow side. It splits a task into a fixed sequence of steps, and each call processes the output of the previous call. It works when the task can be split easily and clearly into subtasks that you know in advance. A repeated code review that uses the same checklist every time is a natural fit.

Adding tests to an undocumented legacy module is the opposite situation. Nobody can list the subtasks before the agent looks at the code. The agent must first map the structure with tools like Glob and Grep. It must find which modules lack coverage and give priority to the risky ones. It must also adapt when it finds something new, for example an external API dependency that needs a mock before any test can run. This is dynamic adaptive decomposition. Anthropic documents this shape as the orchestrator-workers pattern. In this pattern, subtasks are not predefined. They are decided based on what the input and the intermediate results show. This has a real cost: dynamic approaches use more time and more tokens than a fixed pipeline. For this reason, Anthropic advises using the simplest structure that the task allows. In this scenario, the task is open-ended, and that is what justifies the extra flexibility.

Each incorrect approach misses this point. A fixed chain locks in steps that cannot predict what the agent will discover. A single giant prompt gives up decomposition, spreads the model's attention across too much content, and still cannot adapt during the task. Confidence self-rating with retries adjusts output quality, but it does not address the decomposition problem. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate code, and automate repetitive tasks. It uses the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) and integrates with Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

QUESTION: The agent's system prompt instructs it to read the team's conventions file before generating any boilerplate files. Logs show that in 8% of runs it calls Write without reading the conventions first, producing code that breaks the conventions. What change guarantees the required ordering?
answers: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing the conventions file being read before every Write.
Restate the ordering rule at the top of the system prompt in capitalized, emphatic wording.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks Write calls until the conventions file has been read in the session.
Add a PostToolUse hook on Write that detects when the conventions file was skipped and alerts Claude.
feedbacks: Few-shot examples can raise the rate of correct behavior. But they work because the model copies a pattern, and the model can still skip the step sometimes. When the requirement is a guaranteed order, guidance based on examples cannot reach 100%.

Stronger wording is still prompt guidance. The model follows prompt guidance probabilistically, not deterministically. The current 8% failure rate already shows that instructions alone do not guarantee the sequence.

A PreToolUse hook runs before the tool executes, and it can deny the call completely. So a Write can never proceed until the required Read has happened. This changes the ordering rule from probabilistic prompt compliance into a deterministic guarantee enforced by code.

A PostToolUse hook fires only after the tool has already executed. By the time the hook runs, the file that breaks the conventions has already been written. The hook can send corrective context back to the model, but it cannot guarantee the order that the scenario requires.
prompt.explanation:
This question tests the difference between programmatic enforcement and prompt-based guidance. Anything you put in a system prompt, including emphatic wording, repeated rules, or few-shot examples, affects the model's behavior statistically. It raises the probability that the model complies, but it never makes a violation impossible. A PreToolUse hook is a different kind of mechanism, not just a stronger version of the same one. It is code that runs at a fixed point in the agent lifecycle, before the tool call executes, and it can deny the call completely. The model may still try to write a file before it reads the conventions, but that attempt cannot succeed. In practice, this is what a guarantee means.

The timing of hook events explains why the PostToolUse option fails, even though it is also a programmatic mechanism. PostToolUse fires after a tool call completes successfully. This makes it a good fit for changing or annotating results, running formatters, or sending feedback back to the model. But it cannot prevent an action that has already happened. So the choice between PreToolUse and PostToolUse depends on whether you need to prevent something or to react to it. For workflow ordering requirements, the goal is prevention.

The key idea for design reviews is this. Use prompts for preferences and nuance, where an occasional deviation is acceptable. Use hooks wherever a rule must hold on every run, including the runs that nobody is watching. See Claude Code hooks reference, Agent SDK hooks, and the note in Manage Claude's memory that says instruction files are treated as context, not as enforced configuration.

QUESTION: Engineers operating this system want an audit trail recording every subagent the main agent spawns and when each one completes, captured reliably even on unattended runs. Which implementation provides this?
answers: Have each subagent write its own completion entry to a shared log file as its final step.
Instruct the agent in its system prompt to announce every subagent it spawns and summarize each completion.
Parse the agent's final response text for mentions of subagent activity and store any matches.
Register "SubagentStart" and "SubagentStop" hooks that log each delegation and completion as they fire.
feedbacks: This depends on each subagent remembering to write the entry, and that is also probabilistic prompt compliance. A subagent that fails with an error leaves no record. This approach also spreads the logging across many subagents. It does not capture events at the orchestration layer, where every delegation is visible.

Prompt instructions are probabilistic. The model may leave out an announcement, especially during long unattended runs. An audit trail that must be reliable needs a mechanism in code, not compliance that the model can forget.

Inferring system behavior by scanning natural-language output is an anti-pattern. The final response may summarize, leave out, or rephrase details about delegation. This approach observes what the model chose to say, not what actually happened.

These are documented Agent SDK lifecycle hook events. They run your code at the orchestration level whenever a subagent starts or finishes, no matter what the model chooses to say. The SubagentStop input includes identifying fields such as the agent ID and the transcript path. The related tool-use ID is available as a separate parameter of the hook callback. Together, these let you build a complete audit trail where each entry is linked to its delegation.
prompt.explanation:
The principle behind this question is the difference between code-level observation and probabilistic compliance. The Claude Agent SDK fires lifecycle hook events at fixed points in the agent loop. SubagentStart and SubagentStop are the documented mechanism for observing delegation at the orchestration level. They call your callback when a subagent begins or ends. This happens whether or not anyone is watching the session, and whether or not the model mentions the delegation in its text. The SubagentStopHookInput carries identifying metadata, including agent_id, agent_type, and agent_transcript_path. The tool-use ID that started the subagent is passed to the hook callback as a separate tool_use_id (or toolUseID) parameter. So each log entry can still be linked back to the exact delegation in the conversation. Hooks are code, not instructions that the model follows. This makes them much more dependable for audit requirements than any prompt-based approach. But like any callback, they are subject to normal failure and timeout handling, and SubagentStop does not block on failure. So your logging code still needs to be reliable.

The other options all depend on model behavior to produce the audit trail. A system prompt instruction to announce delegations will be followed most of the time. But any single missed announcement damages the record without anyone noticing, and unattended runs are where no one notices the gap. Parsing the final response for mentions of subagent work is a form of a well-known anti-pattern: treating natural-language output as a system signal. The parent agent receives each subagent's final report, but it may summarize or leave out that report. So the text is an unreliable measure of what actually ran. Having each subagent log itself moves the same probabilistic problem down one level. A subagent that crashes, times out, or skips the step leaves no entry. The records are also spread out, instead of being captured at the coordination layer, where every start and completion is visible.

A useful way to think about this: in a hub-and-spoke system, the coordinator and the hooks together form the point where you can observe everything. The coordinator sees every delegation, and hooks turn those lifecycle events into log entries that your code controls. See the Agent SDK hooks guide and the Subagents in the SDK documentation.

QUESTION: While tracing empty-interface usage through a legacy Go service, the agent calls Grep with the pattern "interface{}", and the call fails with a regex diagnostic error. What should the agent do to complete the search?
answers: Escape the curly braces in the pattern, since Grep interprets patterns as regular expressions.
Set "multiline" to true so a pattern containing braces can match across line boundaries.
Switch to Glob for the search, since brace characters belong to file path matching syntax.
Add retry logic around the call, since rejected patterns are usually transient tool errors.
feedbacks: Grep patterns use ripgrep regular expression syntax. So characters like curly braces are regex metacharacters, not literal text. Escaping them, as in the pattern interface\{\}, makes the search match the literal string and fixes the diagnostic error.

The multiline option controls whether a pattern can match across several lines. It does not change how regex metacharacters are parsed. The pattern was rejected because the braces, as written, are invalid regex syntax. Multiline matching does not fix that.

Glob finds files by name or extension pattern. It cannot search inside file contents for a code construct. The task is a content search, which is what Grep is for. Changing tools gives up the correct mechanism.

A rejected pattern is a deterministic syntax error, not a temporary failure. Retrying the same malformed pattern will fail every time. Retries are appropriate for timeouts and temporary unavailability, not for invalid input.
prompt.explanation:
Claude Code's Grep tool is built on ripgrep. This means every pattern it receives is parsed as a regular expression, not as a plain text string. Characters such as curly braces, dots, parentheses, and square brackets have special meaning in regex. So in a code construct like Go's empty interface, the braces must be escaped before the pattern is valid. The documentation uses this same example: to find interface{}, you write interface\{\}. When a pattern cannot be parsed, Grep returns an error that contains ripgrep's diagnostic. This is the signal the agent saw in this scenario.

Grep gives up the simplicity of fixed-string matching to get the power of regex. An agent can search for import statements, error identifiers, or call sites with flexible patterns. But it must treat punctuation inside identifiers as syntax that needs escaping. This happens often during codebase exploration, because real code contains many regex metacharacters.

Each of the other approaches misunderstands the failure. The multiline option controls whether a valid pattern may match across line boundaries. It has no effect on how metacharacters are parsed. Glob works on file names and paths, not file contents, so it cannot find where a construct appears inside code. Retrying is only useful for temporary failures like timeouts. A malformed pattern is a deterministic error, and it will be rejected on every attempt until the pattern itself is corrected.

See the Claude Code tools reference for Grep's regex behavior and the escaping example.

QUESTION: To make the agent use another tool instead of Grep for symbol searches across repositories, the team added a system prompt rule: always use the MCP "code_search" tool instead of Grep. The agent now calls "code_search" even for simple single-file string lookups, producing slow results full of irrelevant matches. What is the best fix?
answers: Add harness logic that reruns any poor "code_search" result through Grep automatically before returning it to the agent.
Introduce a routing tool the agent must call first, which returns the name of the correct search tool for each query.
Keep the system prompt rule and add a permission deny rule that removes Grep from the agent's toolset entirely.
Replace the always-apply rule with boundary language in the "code_search" description stating when each search tool applies.
feedbacks: Rerunning results after the wrong tool has already executed treats the symptom, not the cause. It adds delay and extra calls to every misrouted search. It also gives the agent no better information at the moment it chooses a tool, so the misrouting continues.

A routing tool adds an extra call to every search. It also only moves the selection decision into another tool, and the agent must still call that tool correctly. Clear boundaries in the descriptions solve the routing problem directly, without this extra machinery.

Removing Grep would force every search through the MCP tool, including the simple single-file lookups where Grep is the right choice. This would make the over-use problem happen on every search. Availability controls are for tools that should never be used. They are not for tools that are appropriate in some cases.

Tool descriptions are the main information the model uses when it selects a tool. The documented guidance says a good description covers both when to use a tool and when not to use it. Boundary language sends cross-repository lookups to the MCP tool and leaves simple local searches to Grep. This removes the over-triggering that the always-apply rule caused.
prompt.explanation:
Tool descriptions are the main selection mechanism that an agent uses when it decides which tool to call. Anthropic's guidance says a strong description explains what a tool does and what it returns. It should also explain when to use the tool and when not to use it. In this scenario, two tools overlap: a cross-repository MCP search tool and the built-in Grep. When tools overlap, the rule for when each one applies belongs in the description itself, because that is the text the model reads at the moment it selects a tool.

The always-apply system prompt rule shows a documented anti-pattern. Broad "always use X" instructions tend to over-trigger. They push the tool into cases it was never meant to handle. Explicit direction toward tools is useful, but it should be conditional and specific. Boundary language such as "use this tool for searches spanning multiple repositories; for a string lookup in a single local file, Grep is faster and more appropriate" gives the model a rule for deciding, instead of a fixed command.

Each of the other approaches misses the selection problem. Denying Grep removes a tool that is correct for local lookups. This makes the agent worse instead of guiding it. Rerunning poor results through Grep pays the cost of the wrong call first and only then corrects it. A dedicated routing tool rebuilds the routing function that descriptions already perform, and it adds extra delay and a new point of failure.

See Define tools for description best practices and Claude prompting best practices for guidance on directing tool use without over-prompting.

QUESTION: Despite detailed, distinct tool descriptions, your agent calls a search tool on purely conversational questions and routes code searches between two tools inconsistently. Reviewing the system prompt, you find it states "Always call a tool first before responding" and contains two sections that each name a different tool as the mandatory choice for code searches. Which TWO findings should your review flag? (Select TWO.)
answers: Flag the absence of few-shot examples demonstrating which tool should handle each request type.
Flag the instruction "Always call a tool first before responding" that applies to every request.
Flag the two sections that each name a different tool as the mandatory choice for code search tasks.
Flag that the system prompt comes after the tool definitions in the final prompt.
feedbacks: Descriptions, not examples, are the main selection mechanism, and the descriptions in this scenario are already detailed and distinct. Missing examples would not cause the model to call tools on conversational turns. They would also not cause it to switch randomly between tools. The instructions that misdirect the model would still be there even if examples were added.

A blanket "always call a tool" instruction pushes the model toward tool calls, even on conversational turns where a direct answer is appropriate. This matches the over-triggering symptom. Anthropic's guidance treats this kind of wording as prompt-based direction of tool use. When a tool call must happen, the mechanism to use is tool_choice, not broad prompt wording.

When two instructions contradict each other, Claude may follow either one at random. This produces the inconsistent routing seen in this scenario. System prompt text is combined with the tool definitions. So these conflicting instructions can override the selection that the well-written descriptions would otherwise produce.

The documented template does place the user system prompt after the tool definitions. But that is the normal, intended structure, not a defect. The system prompt still has a strong effect on tool behavior from that position. So this placement cannot explain either symptom.
prompt.explanation:
When a request includes tools, the API builds a single tool-use system prompt. It combines the tool definitions in JSON Schema, the user-specified system prompt, and the tool configuration. In practice, this means your system prompt text and your tool descriptions end up in the same context, and together they drive tool selection. So stronger instructions elsewhere in the prompt can still override a well-written description. This is why reviewing the system prompt is an important debugging step when tool behavior goes wrong even though the descriptions are good.

Two failure patterns stand out in this review. The first is a blanket instruction such as "Always call a tool first before responding". This is a documented form of prompt-based direction. It pushes the model to call tools even on conversational turns where no tool is needed, and this causes over-triggering. Anthropic's guidance is to keep this kind of wording proportionate. When a tool call must be guaranteed, and not just encouraged, use tool_choice. The second pattern is two sections that each declare a different tool mandatory for the same task. This is a contradiction, and Claude may pick either one at random on any turn. That is why the routing looks random even though each description is clear on its own.

The other findings are not valid. The user system prompt comes after the tool definitions because that is the documented template order, and this order does not weaken its influence. Few-shot examples are a secondary aid. Anthropic's guidance is to put detailed descriptions first, and this system already has them. See Tool use overview, Define tools, and Claude prompting best practices.

QUESTION: While automating a repetitive migration task, an agent discovers an undocumented external API dependency mid-run and adds a mocking subtask that was never part of its original plan. Which loop design makes this adaptive behavior possible?
answers: Enable extended thinking so the model anticipates all contingencies, including hidden dependencies, before execution begins.
Feed each tool result back into the model so it chooses the next action based on what was discovered.
Run the loop with no turn limit so the agent keeps iterating until every subtask completes.
Enumerate every possible subtask during initial planning and activate whichever ones match conditions at runtime.
feedbacks: Extended thinking adds more reasoning before a response. But it cannot reveal facts that only tool execution can show, such as a dependency hidden in the code. The agent adapts by reacting to the results it observes, not by predicting everything in advance.

This is the core of the agentic loop. After every tool execution, the result is returned to Claude. Claude evaluates the updated state and decides what to do next. Each decision uses everything the agent has discovered so far. So the agent can create subtasks that no upfront plan expected, such as mocking a newly found dependency.

By default, the SDK sets no maximum number of tool-use turns. But a loop with no limit only allows more iterations. It does not explain how the agent changes its plan. That comes from feeding tool results back into the model's decisions.

This describes a hard-coded decision tree, where all branches must be known in advance. That is the opposite of decisions made by the model. An undocumented dependency could never appear in a subtask list written in advance. So this design cannot explain the observed behavior.
prompt.explanation:
The Claude Agent SDK runs an autonomous agent loop. The model evaluates the current state, calls a tool, and receives the result. It repeats this until it produces a response with no more tool calls. The most important property is that every tool result goes back into the model's context before the next decision. So the plan is never fixed. The model works it out again on each iteration from everything it has observed so far. When a Grep or Read result shows an undocumented external API, that discovery is new evidence for the next decision. The model can respond by creating a subtask, such as adding a mock, that no one specified at the start. This is why the exam material separates dynamic adaptive decomposition from fixed pipelines. In dynamic adaptive decomposition, subtasks are created from intermediate results, and it suits open-ended investigations. In a fixed pipeline, every step is decided in advance.

Each incorrect option names the wrong source of adaptive behavior. Listing all subtasks in advance is a hard-coded decision tree. It only handles situations that someone predicted, and this defeats the purpose of investigating unknowns. Extended thinking adds deeper reasoning, but it cannot reveal facts that only tool execution shows. It is true that the loop has no default limit on tool-use turns (you can set a limit with max_turns). But unlimited iterations only allow more steps. They do not cause the agent to change its plan. Decisions based on what the agent observes do that.

The key idea is to think of the loop as reason, act, observe. The observe step is what turns a fixed plan into an adaptive investigation. See The Agent Loop and the Claude Agent SDK overview for how tool results drive each next decision.

QUESTION: The coordinator delegates codebase survey subtasks to parallel subagents, but completed surveys repeatedly omit entire subsystems even though every subagent finishes its assignment successfully. Which two changes most effectively address this coverage problem? (Select TWO.)
answers: Move the subagents to a model with a larger context window so each one can analyze more files per task.
Instruct each subagent to broaden its investigation beyond its assigned area whenever it encounters related code paths.
Have the coordinator review the aggregated findings for coverage gaps and delegate follow-up subtasks to fill them.
Have the coordinator give each subagent an explicit objective and boundaries so the subtasks together span the codebase.
feedbacks: A larger context window changes how much each subagent can read within its assignment. But subagents only investigate what they are asked to investigate. If no subtask ever mentions a subsystem, more capacity for each agent will not bring that subsystem into the survey.

Letting subagents go beyond their assignments does not guarantee that unassigned subsystems get covered. Mostly, it produces duplicated work and overlapping findings. Coverage must be designed at the coordinator level, where the full scope is visible. It should not be left to workers that see only part of the scope.

An iterative refinement loop lets the coordinator compare the combined results against the original goal. The coordinator can then find subsystems that no subagent investigated, and start more subagents to cover those gaps. This is the documented orchestrator pattern of improving the strategy after receiving findings.

Incomplete coverage starts in the coordinator's decomposition, not in how the subagents execute. Give each subagent a clear objective and explicit task boundaries. Design the assignments so that together they divide up the full survey scope. This prevents whole areas from never being assigned to anyone.
prompt.explanation:
In a coordinator-subagent (orchestrator-worker) architecture, the coordinator's task decomposition sets the outer limit of what the system can discover. Subagents are separate agent instances with isolated context. Each one sees only the prompt it was given, works within it, and returns a final summary. If every subagent succeeds but whole subsystems are missing from the output, the failure happened earlier, in how the work was divided. Nothing in a subagent's design lets it notice that an assignment for another subagent was never created.

Anthropic's engineering write-up on its multi-agent research system says this directly. The lead agent must give each subagent an objective, an output format, guidance on tools, and clear task boundaries. Otherwise, subagents will duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. The two effective fixes act at the two points where the coordinator has control. Before delegation, the coordinator should design the subtasks so that their boundaries together cover the entire target, the way a surveyor divides an area of land into parts. After the results return, it should run an iterative refinement loop. It compares the combined findings against the original goal, finds gaps, and starts more subagents for the missed areas. The documented orchestrator pattern includes this step: the lead agent combines the findings and may create more subagents or change its strategy if coverage is incomplete.

The other options fix the wrong layer. Telling subagents to go beyond their assignments replaces a coverage problem with a duplication problem. It still leaves unassigned areas to chance, because no single worker can see the full scope. A larger context window for each subagent increases how much it can process within its task. But the breadth of the survey is set by what the coordinator asks for, not by the capacity of each agent.

See How we built our multi-agent research system and Subagents in the SDK for the details of delegation and context isolation.

QUESTION: While the agent is exploring a legacy codebase, a Bash tool call it requested fails with a permission error. How should your loop report this failure before the next request to Claude?
answers: Retry the identical Bash call automatically until it succeeds before sending anything back to Claude.
Return a "tool_result" block with "is_error" set to true containing the error message, then continue the loop.
End the loop and show the raw error to the engineer, since the agent cannot continue without that output.
Append the error text as a new assistant message so Claude sees the failure in its own conversation turn.
feedbacks: Silent retries with no limit waste time and tokens. They will never succeed for failures that are not temporary, such as a permission error. The loop should report the failure, so that Claude can decide on another approach instead of repeating a call that cannot succeed.

This is the documented pattern for client-side tool failures. The error goes back as a tool result marked with the error flag, and this keeps the message structure valid. Claude can then reason about the failure and try to recover, for example by trying a different command or path.

Ending the whole loop because of a single tool failure is an anti-pattern. It removes the agent's ability to recover. Claude can work around many failures, such as a permission error on one path, if it receives the error as a tool result.

Tool outcomes must be returned as tool result blocks in a user message. That user message must come directly after the assistant message that contains the tool call. Adding the error as made-up assistant text breaks the required message structure. It also breaks the link to the tool call that caused the error.
prompt.explanation:
In the agentic loop, a failed tool execution is still a tool outcome. The model expects to receive it in the same way as a success. The documented approach is to return a tool_result block whose tool_use_id refers to the original call. Set is_error to true and put the error details in the content. The loop then continues in the same way as after a successful call. Claude reads the error, reasons about it, and decides the next action. That action might be trying a different command, reading the file with the Read tool instead, or explaining the limitation. Anthropic's documentation notes that Claude includes such errors in its response and can retry with corrections when the problem can be fixed.

The harness never edits the conversation for Claude. It only executes the tools that Claude requests and adds the results. That is why writing the error into a made-up assistant message is wrong. Tool results must arrive in a user message that comes directly after the assistant message containing the tool_use block. If you break that pairing, the history becomes invalid or misleading. The other wrong options are errors of judgment, not of structure. Ending the entire loop because of one failure throws away the agent's main strength, which is recovering on its own. It is the same anti-pattern as stopping a multi-agent workflow when a single subagent fails. Silent retries with no limit are worse than useless for errors that cannot be fixed by retrying, such as permission denials. A limited number of retries can make sense for temporary failures. But in the end, the model should be told what happened, so it can choose another path.

See Handle tool calls for how is_error works and the rules for message order, and How tool use works for the full agentic loop.

Keeping the coordinator as the hub keeps the main benefits of hub-and-spoke orchestration. Every exchange can be observed in one place. Failures are handled by one component that has full context about the workflow. The coordinator also decides which findings each subagent needs. These benefits are more important than the small delay of an extra routing step.

Self-rated confidence is an unreliable measure of quality. Auditing afterward does not give the coordinator real-time visibility into the exchange. It also does not give the coordinator control over what information each subagent receives. The design weaknesses of the direct hand-off remain.

First, the coordinator can observe every interaction, which is essential for debugging and monitoring a production system. Second, it can apply uniform error handling, with full knowledge of the overall workflow state. Third, it can select what information goes to each subagent. It can remove irrelevant detail and add needed constraints before it delegates. A small cost in delay gives a large gain in control and reliability.

The way the Claude Agent SDK works supports this design. A standard subagent is a separate agent instance with its own fresh context window. It receives only its own system prompt and the prompt that the coordinator passes when it starts the subagent. Its intermediate work stays inside its own context, and only a final report returns to the caller. This is why the belief that both subagents already share the coordinator's history is wrong. It is also why the coordinator is the natural place to collect findings and send them on. Some documented modes let agents message each other more directly, such as agent teams. But when a team has chosen a hub-and-spoke design for an agentic workflow, the reason for that choice is to keep routing central.

Retry logic inside subagents is a useful addition for temporary failures. It does not replace visibility at the coordinator level. Self-rated confidence scores do not reliably reflect output quality. The interview pattern is the more direct technique when the goal is to draw out design decisions that the engineer has not yet stated, such as the invalidation strategy.

The interview pattern is designed for this situation. When the developer has not thought about key design considerations, Claude asks targeted questions about technical implementation, edge cases, and tradeoffs. This brings out issues like the cache invalidation strategy and failure modes before any code is written.

A detailed specification only covers considerations the engineer has already thought of. In this scenario, the invalidation strategy and failure modes have not been considered. So a spec written up front, without Claude's questions, would carry the same gaps in understanding into the implementation.

Concrete input and output examples are the right tool when the developer already knows the expected transformation and needs to communicate it accurately. This scenario is the opposite. The requirements themselves are not known yet, so there is nothing well defined to show with examples.
prompt.explanation:
The interview pattern reverses the usual direction of a coding session. Usually the developer specifies and Claude executes. In this pattern, Claude asks the questions. Anthropic documents this as "Let Claude interview you". You start with a minimal prompt. Claude then asks about technical implementation, edge cases, concerns, and tradeoffs before it writes any code. Then you record the answers in a written spec. The pattern exists because developers who work in unfamiliar domains almost always have gaps in what they know. They cannot write a complete specification for things they have not yet thought of. Cache invalidation and failure modes are classic examples. A model that has implemented many caching layers knows which questions to ask. The engineer may not know which answers matter until someone asks.

The tempting alternative is plan mode, and it is related. Both delay implementation until the design is settled, and Claude can ask clarifying questions while it plans. The difference is focus. The purpose of plan mode is to have Claude research the codebase and present a proposed approach for approval. Any questions along the way only support producing that plan. In the interview pattern, systematic questioning is the explicit goal. This is why it is the more direct technique when the gap is requirements that nobody has stated yet. The two work well together: interview first to settle the requirements, and then plan or execute. Concrete input and output examples solve a different problem: they communicate a transformation that the developer already understands. An upfront spec written by the developer only records the gaps in knowledge that already exist.

The allowedTools setting on the parent options auto-approves tool calls. It is not a restriction for each subagent. The subagent would still inherit Write and Bash and could continue to modify files, because nothing in this change removes those tools from its session.

The tools field in an AgentDefinition is an allowlist for that subagent. Tools that are not on the list are not present in the subagent's session. So Write and Bash become impossible to call, not just discouraged. This is the design-level control for limiting a subagent to its role.
prompt.explanation:
In the Claude Agent SDK, each subagent is defined with an AgentDefinition, and its tools field acts as an allowlist. When the field is omitted, the subagent inherits every tool that is available to subagents. This is how an exploration agent ends up with Write and Bash, which it was never meant to use. When the field is filled in, any tool that is not listed is completely absent from that subagent's session. Claude does not see the tool, cannot request it, and gets no permission prompt for it. This makes the restriction deterministic: misuse becomes impossible by design, not just unlikely.

The same scoping principle applies to how tools are given to agents in general. A subagent that has tools outside its specialization tends to use them, because they are available. Removing the capability in the definition is a stronger control than any fix applied later. The parent-level allowedTools option is a different mechanism. It auto-approves tool calls so they run without a prompt. But it does not remove tools from the set a subagent inherits, so it cannot stop the unwanted writes. A system prompt ban depends on the model following instructions, and the observed behavior already shows that it does not do this consistently. An audit-logging hook is useful for understanding what happened. But it acts after the fact and blocks nothing.

Have the per-file stage return structured findings constrained by a JSON schema instead of prose.

feedbacks: Combining the chain into one pass brings back the problem of attention spread across many files, which staged review exists to avoid. It also removes the intermediate outputs that you can inspect. Those outputs make a chained pipeline easier to debug and evaluate.

If the per-file stage must follow a JSON schema, it produces compact, predictable intermediate results. The integration pass can use these results reliably. This fixes the hand-off at its source. The integration stage receives only the essential findings, in a known shape, instead of long prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data) that it must search through.

An instruction to be brief is probabilistic. The model may still produce long free-form text or free-form text with an inconsistent format. The output shape stays unpredictable for the next stage. When a later stage must process intermediate results programmatically, output constrained by a schema is the dependable mechanism.

A larger context window lets more tokens fit. But it does not help the model pay reliable attention to long, unstructured findings spread across the input. The problem is the quality and shape of the intermediate data, not the space to hold it.
prompt.explanation:
In an explicit prompt chain, each stage is a separate call. The quality of the whole pipeline depends heavily on the hand-off between stages. A review chain that does per-file analysis and then integration works because the first stage reduces each file to its findings. The second stage then reasons only over those findings. If the first stage produces long free-form text, the integration stage receives a large, irregular input, and most of the benefit of staging is lost. The model must search through unstructured text for the facts that matter, and it misses connections between files.

The documented fix is to make the intermediate results structured. You can constrain the per-file stage with a JSON schema (for example, with output_config and a json_schema format). This guarantees that the output is valid JSON with a known shape. The integration pass then receives consistent fields such as file name, issue, severity, and evidence, instead of prose (ordinary sentences, not structured data). Note the limit of that guarantee: a schema enforces structure, not the correctness of the values. Chains move data between calls. Whenever a later call processes an earlier call's output programmatically, design that output like an interface, not like a story.

A larger context window adds capacity, but it does not improve attention over disorganized input. Merging the stages into one prompt removes the chain completely. Describe the two interacting fixes together in one message, then fix the naming issue in a follow-up.
Send each of the three fixes one at a time, letting Claude fully complete each before starting the next.

feedbacks: Starting a new session is the documented fix when a session is full of repeated failed corrections. It is not the first response to normal review findings. In this scenario, the existing session context about the endpoint is still valid and useful.

When two fixes depend on each other, Claude needs to see both requirements at the same time. Then it can design one solution that meets both of them. The naming issue is independent and has no such dependency. So it can be handled afterward, with no risk of rework.

Sending fixes one at a time works for independent issues. But if you apply one of two interacting fixes on its own, the second fix must then partly undo it. The dependent changes should be given together, so that Claude can meet both constraints in a single pass.

Parallel subagents are documented for independent investigations whose paths do not depend on each other. Two fixes that depend on each other would be made in separate contexts, and neither context could see the other. This produces conflicting edits.
prompt.explanation:
The principle is that the way you group feedback should match the dependencies between the fixes. Sometimes two changes depend on each other. For example, the validation logic decides which error cases exist, and the error response format must represent those cases. In that situation, Claude needs to see both requirements at the same time to produce a design that meets both. If you give them one at a time, Claude may find a solution that only works for the first fix. It implements the first fix without knowing about the second, and the second fix then forces rework of the first. An independent issue, such as an inconsistent name, shares no design decisions with the other fixes. So handling it in a separate later step is simpler and keeps each message focused.

The same reasoning is behind Anthropic's guidance on strong prompts. Fixing one issue at a time is the right approach for independent issues, but it guarantees repeated rework on connected ones. This fixes the root cause. Claude focused too much on making the tests pass, and it treated the test inputs as the full specification. Anthropic's guidance is to ask explicitly for a general-purpose implementation that works for all valid inputs. The tests should serve as verification, not as the definition of the solution.

Raw self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated. The model can be confident and wrong, especially on the hard cases. Confidence scores are only useful for routing after they have been calibrated against a labeled validation set. So acting on a threshold without first testing it in that way is unsafe.

Stratified random sampling intentionally measures error rates inside the group of entries that would be automated. It catches rare or new error patterns that purely random sampling or an overall score would miss. This gives direct evidence about whether high-confidence outputs are actually safe to stop reviewing.
prompt.explanation:
The main trap in this situation is trusting an aggregate metric. A 97% overall accuracy can exist together with, for example, a 40% error rate on one specific pull request category or one output field. This happens because the many easy cases hide the failing segment in the average. Before human review is reduced, accuracy must be segmented. That means it is measured separately by input type and by each field. Then the team knows whether performance is strong everywhere or only strong on average. Anthropic's evaluation guidance makes the same point about how to build eval sets. Eval sets should reflect the real mix of tasks, including edge cases, so that weaknesses in a segment become visible and are not hidden by the average. See Create strong empirical evaluations.

The second necessary step is stratified random sampling of the entries that would no longer be reviewed, which are the high-confidence ones. Random sampling across all output tends to pick too many easy cases, and it misses rare but important error patterns. Stratifying by confidence band directly measures the error rate inside the group that would be automated. That is the only number that actually justifies removing a reviewer.

Structured state persistence is the documented pattern for crash recovery. Each agent or phase writes its status and findings to a known location. Long-running agent work with several phases needs structured state persistence to survive crashes. On restart, the coordinator loads the manifest first and sends out only the unfinished work. The manifest itself is not a built-in feature. Getting completion status from it means re-reading long output, instead of checking reliable data. Content in the root CLAUDE.md always loads into every session, and that is what the team wants to avoid. The infrastructure conventions would then use context during frontend or documentation work, where they are irrelevant.

Conflicting values from credible sources are useful information, not noise. The subagent should include both figures, with their source documents and an explicit note that they conflict. This gives the main session, which has broader context, everything it needs to decide how to reconcile them before the combined documentation is written.

Passing both values without marking them as conflicting hides the disagreement. A later step may then pick one value or mix them without noticing. The conflict must be marked explicitly, so that it is handled on purpose and not resolved by accident.

A documented conflict between two credible sources is not a failure that justifies stopping the work. The subagent can complete its analysis and report the conflict with sources. This keeps the value of the completed work and still sends the reconciliation decision up to the main session.

Its intermediate tool calls and discoveries stay inside it, and only the final message returns to the parent. This design keeps long analysis out of the main session's context window. The correct handling of conflicting source data follows a consistent pattern: complete the work, keep both values, name the source of each, and mark the conflict explicitly. The layer with the broadest context then does the reconciliation on purpose. In this scenario, that layer is the main session acting as coordinator. An explicit request for human handling is a top-priority reason to escalate, and the agent should follow it immediately. Ignoring the stated instruction in order to show what the agent can do, even on an easy issue, goes against what the requester clearly asked for. It also reduces trust in the automation.

Running diagnostics is still investigation, and the ticket explicitly prohibited investigation. Work done for the handoff, even with good intentions, ignores the requester's instruction. The handoff should contain the ticket contents and the reason for escalation, not new analysis.
prompt.explanation:
Escalation design separates two kinds of cases. In the first kind, the agent should try to resolve the case, because it is within the agent's scope. In the second kind, the agent should escalate immediately. An explicit request for a human always belongs to the second kind. The instruction itself is the decision. The agent does not need to investigate, estimate how hard the issue is, or show that it could have fixed it. Acting anyway, even for a short time, puts the system's judgment in place of the requester's stated preference. This damages trust in the automation much more than skipping one easy fix ever could.

The tempting middle option is to gather diagnostics "for the handoff." It fails for the same reason: diagnostics are investigation, and the ticket prohibited investigation. A good handoff is built from what the agent already has (the ticket text and the reason for escalation). It is not built from new work done against instructions. The attempt-first option uses the right pattern in the wrong kind of case. Trying to resolve before escalating is appropriate only when there is no explicit request for a human. Confidence self-rating fails for a different reason. Models are poorly calibrated about their own reliability. Also, no indirect measure is needed in this scenario, because the requester already gave a clear signal.

QUESTION: The project CLAUDE.md holds your team's rules for writing useful tests, but people have since added a copied framework tutorial, a full API reference, and long test-runner documentation. Generated tests now often ignore those rules. What change most reliably makes Claude follow the rules again?
answers: Move the testing standards into each developer's user-level CLAUDE.md so they load with less clutter.
Duplicate the testing criteria at both the top and bottom of the file so Claude notices them.
Trim the file to concise testing standards, removing material Claude can infer from the code.
Prefix every testing rule with IMPORTANT so the criteria outrank the reference material around them.
feedbacks: User-level memory applies only to one person, and version control does not share it. So team standards would become different between developers, or new teammates would miss them. It also still loads together with the overloaded project file, so the extra content remains.

Duplicating content makes the file even longer. It does nothing about the tutorial and reference material that hide the rules. The documented fix for an overloaded CLAUDE.md is to cut low-value content, not to repeat the high-value content.

Every line in CLAUDE.md competes for the model's attention, and an overloaded file causes Claude to ignore the instructions that matter. Removing tutorials, API references, and other content that Claude can infer or find in the codebase makes the rules for useful tests stand out again.

Emphasis only raises a rule's priority compared with less emphasized rules near it. When every line is marked important, no line stands out. This also does not fix the real problem, which is a file full of material that Claude could infer.
prompt.explanation:
CLAUDE.md is guidance, not enforced configuration. Its contents are loaded as context at the start of every session, and the model weighs every line against every other line. This design makes the file powerful, because the project knowledge is always present. It also makes the file fragile when it grows too large. Anthropic's guidance says clearly that an overgrown CLAUDE.md causes Claude to ignore the important instructions. The file should leave out things Claude can infer from the code, detailed API documentation, long tutorials, and obvious advice. A copied framework tutorial and a full API reference are in that category. They add tokens but no judgment, and they weaken the rules for useful tests that the team actually needs Claude to follow.

CLAUDE.md has a fixed amount of attention to spend. Short rules that can be checked (which test runner to use, what makes a test useful to write, which fixtures exist) use that attention well. Reference material that Claude could read from the repository uses it badly. This is why removing content makes Claude follow the rules again, while the other approaches fail. Duplicating the criteria makes the file even longer. Emphasis markers on every rule like IMPORTANT only work compared with less emphasized rules around them. Moving the standards to each developer's user-level file stops sharing the team conventions, and it does not reduce what loads into the session. If some testing material is long or only sometimes relevant, the documented pattern is to move it into a skill or a path-scoped rule. Then it loads on demand instead of in every session.

See Claude Code Best Practices for what belongs in CLAUDE.md and Manage Claude's memory for memory scopes and modular organization.

QUESTION: A developer has Claude Code write edge-case tests for a data migration script first (null values, empty strings), then implement the script. When the null-handling test fails, Claude edits that test's expected value so all the tests pass, leaving nulls mishandled. What instruction change most effectively fixes this?
answers: State that the tests must not be removed or edited; they cannot change, so iterate only on the implementation.
Have Claude rate its confidence in each failing test and discard any it rates as likely incorrect.
Add more edge-case examples to the prompt so Claude generalizes better beyond the failing null case.
Start a fresh session and regenerate the implementation repeatedly until one run passes the full suite.
feedbacks: This directly fixes the failure. Claude treated a passing suite as the goal, and it changed the test instead of the code. Anthropic's guidance for test-first workflows is to remind Claude that tests must not be removed or edited, because doing so hides missing or buggy functionality. If the tests are fixed verification criteria, the only way to make a failing test pass is to change the implementation.

Self-rated confidence is unreliable, because the model can be confident and wrong. This approach also makes deleting tests acceptable. It would make it easier, not harder, to drop valid edge-case expectations from the suite.

More examples improve how well the implementation handles varied inputs, but that is a different problem. In this scenario, the test already had the right expectation. The problem is that Claude changed the test instead of fixing the code, and extra examples do not forbid that.

Regenerating again and again does not fix the root cause. Nothing in the prompt tells Claude that it must not change the tests, so any run may again modify a test to make it pass. Retrying without changing the instruction wastes effort and leaves the failure mode in place.
prompt.explanation:
In a test-driven iteration workflow, the test cases are the contract. They define the expected input and output behavior (in this scenario, how null values must be handled). The implementation is the only thing allowed to change until the tests pass. Anthropic's prompting guidance warns that Claude can focus too much on making the suite pass. For longer tasks like migrations, it explicitly recommends having Claude write tests before the implementation. It also recommends reminding Claude that tests should not be removed or edited, because doing so can hide missing or buggy functionality. Adding that one instruction brings back the one-way rule that the workflow depends on: a failing test means you fix the code, and you never rewrite the expectation.

The key idea is the difference between tests as verification and tests as something that can be changed. When the prompt does not say that tests are fixed, a passing suite stops being evidence of correctness. Claude works toward the visible goal (all tests pass) by the cheapest path available. Each incorrect approach misses this. More edge-case examples improve generalization, but they do not protect the existing expectations. Self-rated confidence invites the model to drop tests that are inconvenient, and models can be confident and wrong. Regenerating in new sessions only tries the same unconstrained behavior again, hoping for a different result. Some teams want a hard guarantee instead of an instruction. For them, a PreToolUse hook can block edits to test files completely, because instructions are guidance while hooks are enforcement.

See Claude prompting best practices for guidance on test-first workflows and on treating tests as verification, and Claude Code common workflows for working with tests and edge cases.

QUESTION: Your team adds a custom MCP tool that searches an internal package registry during refactoring sessions, and you are designing how the tool reports failures. Which TWO behaviors enable Claude to make good recovery decisions? (Select TWO.)
answers: Normalize every failure into a single generic unavailable status so Claude's error handling stays simple.
Return an empty match list marked as successful when the registry is unreachable, so the session continues smoothly.
Include any matches retrieved before the failure in the error details sent back to Claude.
Return a distinct error when the registry times out, separate from a successful search with no matches.
feedbacks: A generic status hides the context that Claude needs to choose between retrying, changing the query, or continuing with partial information. It also goes against the documented guidance to return error details that the model can see, which tell Claude what failed and what to try instead.

This is silent error suppression. Claude would conclude that no matching packages exist, when in fact the search never ran. During refactoring, that false conclusion could lead Claude to delete or rename code that is actually in use.

Partial results keep the work that was already completed. They give Claude concrete information to use when it decides whether to retry, narrow the query, or continue with what it has. Throwing them away forces Claude to repeat work, and it removes useful context from the recovery decision.

A timeout and a truly empty result set mean different things, and they need different responses. A timeout may justify a retry. Zero matches is a valid and useful finding. If you mix them up, Claude would retry valid empty searches. Worse, it could treat an unreachable registry as proof that no usages exist.
prompt.explanation:
Error reporting from a tool is not just logging. It is an input to the model's next decision. When a custom MCP tool fails, Anthropic's guidance is to catch the exception yourself and return an error result that the model can see, marked with isError. This result should carry enough context for Claude to understand what failed and what to try instead. Do not let a raw exception or a bare status pass through. (For client-side Messages API tools, the equivalent is a tool_result block with is_error set to true.) The content of that error payload decides whether Claude can recover intelligently or must recover blindly.

Two properties matter most in this scenario. First, the tool must separate access failures from valid empty results. A registry timeout means the question was never answered, and a retry or another approach may succeed. A successful query that matched nothing is a finding in itself. If both look the same to Claude, Claude either wastes loops retrying real empty results, or, much more dangerously, treats an outage as evidence that no code depends on a package. Second, the error should include any partial results that were retrieved before the failure, together with details of what was attempted. This keeps completed work and lets Claude decide between retrying, narrowing the query, or continuing with what it already has, instead of starting over with no information.

The two rejected behaviors damage recovery in different ways. Silent suppression, which returns an empty list marked as successful, turns a failure into a wrong fact that looks certain. In a refactoring workflow, this can lead directly to deleting code that is still used. Generic statuses keep the error-handling code simple. But they throw away the context that recovery decisions depend on: the failure type, the attempted query, and the partial results. This goes against the documented guidance that error results should give Claude enough context to decide whether to retry, change the query, or continue with partial information.

See Custom tools for the Agent SDK recommendation to catch exceptions and return isError results with context instead of raw failures, and Handle tool calls for returning errors from client-side tools with is_error tool results.
